I picked **candidate 1**, with about 50% confidence that it really is the best. It and candidate 5 order almost the same amounts, so the choice between them comes down to how often each one orders. My estimate puts candidate 1 about 70–100 ahead of candidate 5, which is small next to the spread caused by random demand. I worked this out by hand, as you asked, without running a simulation.

**What every plan loses regardless.** On days 0–2 there are only 27 units of product 0 against an average demand of about 55. On days 0–3 there are only 58 units of product 1 against about 120. No plan can avoid these shortages, because the first deliveries can't arrive in time.

**Comparing order cycles.** The daily cost of a cycle of T days is the 39 fee divided by T, plus storage of 0.4 × 51 × (T−1)/2, where 51 is the combined daily demand. That gives:

| Cycle length T | 1 day | 2 days | 3 days | 4 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Daily cost | ≈ 39 | ≈ 29.7 | ≈ 33.4 | ≈ 40.4 |

A 2-day cycle is cheapest, and a 3-day cycle comes next.

- **Candidate 6 (orders every day):** 27 order fees come to about 1,050. That is roughly 500 more in fees than candidate 1, while it saves only about 265 in storage. It also keeps almost no safety stock for product 1.
- **Candidate 3 (every 4 days):** this adds about 530 in storage, and each batch of product 0 covers all 4 days of its shelf life, so anything left over is thrown away. It saves only about 270 in fees.
- **Candidate 4:** it orders product 0 every 2 days but product 1 only every 4 days, so it pays the same fees as candidate 1 with about 340 more storage. Its product 1 orders also equal average demand with no safety margin.

**How much each plan orders, compared with average demand.** Average demand is about 516 units of product 0 and about 939 units of product 1 over the days the orders can serve.

- **Candidates 0 and 2** order about 1,078 units of product 1, roughly 15% above average. Product 1 keeps for 9 days, so the surplus builds up and is mostly wasted, costing about 9 per unit plus storage. Candidate 2 also over-orders product 0, at about 588 units.
- **Candidate 7** orders exactly the forecast for both products. Since demand averages about 4.6% above the forecast, it falls short more often.
- **Candidate 5** (every 3 days) and **candidate 1** (every 2 days) both order about 541 units of product 0 and about 990 of product 1, roughly 5% above average demand.

**Why candidate 1 beats candidate 5.** The 2-day cycle costs about 195 more in order fees but saves about 265 in storage. It also gives leftover product 0 two extra days to sell instead of one, so less of it is wasted.

**Выбор: кандидат 7.** Расчёт приближённый, в уме, на средних значениях спроса; запас над кандидатом 1 (около 300) — оценка, а не точная цифра.

**Чем различаются планы.** Все сравнения — по прогнозу спроса за дни, которые покрывают заказы. Средний фактический спрос выше прогноза примерно на 4,6 %.

| Кандидат | Ритм заказов | Сколько раз платится 39 | Товар 0 к прогнозу | Товар 1 к прогнозу |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | раз в 3 дня | 9 | 1,1 | 1,2 |
| 2 | раз в 3 дня | 9 | 1,2 | 1,2 |
| 5 | раз в 3 дня | 9 | 1,1 | 1,1 |
| 7 | раз в 3 дня | 9 | 1,0 | 1,0 |
| 3 | раз в 4 дня | 7 | ≈1,1 | ≈1,1 |
| 1 | раз в 2 дня | 14 | 1,1 | 1,1 |
| 4 | товар 0 раз в 2 дня, товар 1 раз в 4 дня | 14 | ≈1,1 | ≈1,1 |
| 6 | каждый день | 27 | 1,1 | 1,05 |

**Ритм заказов (сборы против хранения).**
- Каждый лишний день между заказами добавляет около 0,5 дня спроса к среднему запасу. Это примерно 25 единиц × 0,4 × 26 дней ≈ 260 за хранение.
- Ритм в 4 дня (кандидат 3) экономит только 78 на сборах, а платит около 260 за хранение. Кроме того, партия товара 0 живёт ровно 4 дня, переносить остаток некуда, и растёт риск списаний. Проигрывает.
- Ежедневный ритм (кандидат 6) экономит около 260 на хранении, но платит примерно на 500 больше сборов, чем ритм в 2 дня. Проигрывает.
- Ритм в 2 дня (кандидат 1) против 3 дней при одинаковом объёме (кандидат 5): примерно +260 на хранении и −195 на сборах, итого около +65 в пользу кандидата 1.
- Кандидат 4 платит те же 14 сборов, что и кандидат 1, но держит товар 1 запасом на 4 дня. Он хуже кандидата 1 при тех же расходах.
- Склад на 228 единиц почти переполняется только у кандидата 3 (около 222 в день 8). У планов с ритмом 3 дня запас доходит примерно до 200.

**Объём заказа.**
- Каждая лишняя единица стоит 9 (плюс хранение). Она окупается, только если снимает больше 9/16 ≈ 0,56 единицы нехватки у товара 1 и больше 0,5 единицы у товара 0. У товара 1 недопродажа стоит 14 + 2 = 16, у товара 0 — 14 + 4 = 18.
- **Товар 1** хранится 9 дней, поэтому избыток переходит в следующие циклы, и считать нужно общий объём за весь срок. Средний спрос за дни 4–29 около 939 единиц.
  - У кандидата 7 заказано 898: ожидаемая нехватка около 62.
  - У кандидата 5 — 990: нехватка около 22.
  - 92 лишние единицы снимают около 40 единиц нехватки, то есть примерно 0,43 на единицу. Это меньше 0,56.
  - У кандидатов 0 и 2 заказано 1078. Около 140 единиц сверх среднего, которые в основном пропадут.
- **Товар 0:** переход от 1,0 к 1,1 прогноза снимает около 0,4–0,5 единицы нехватки на каждую добавленную единицу. Это на границе окупаемости или ниже, а с учётом хранения и списаний — в минус.

**Итог.** Порядок: 7 > 5 > 0 > 2 при ритме 3 дня. Кандидат 7 опережает кандидата 5 примерно на 400 (около 340 по товару 1 и 80 с лишним по товару 0). Это больше, чем около 65, которые кандидат 1 выигрывает у кандидата 5 за счёт ритма в 2 дня. При отклонениях спроса кандидат 7 тоже устойчивее: склад не переполняется, лишнего товара, который пропадёт, почти нет, а риск нехватки ограничен тем, что спрос у обоих товаров в среднем лишь чуть выше прогноза.

I picked **Candidate 1**. I worked this out roughly in my head from the forecast averages, not with a full day-by-day simulation, so the cost figures below are estimates.

**Where the plans differ.** Total forecast demand is about 546 units of item 0 and 1013 of item 1, so the most margin any plan can earn is about 7,800. Every plan takes the same early shortages, because the starting stock runs out before the first delivery. After that, plans differ mainly in how often they order:

| How often a plan orders | Candidates | Order fees (39 per day) | Extra storage cost (rough) | Total (rough) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Every day | 6 | about 1,050 | about 0 | about 1,050 |
| Every 2 days | 1, 4 | 546 | about 270 | about 816 |
| Every 3 days | 0, 2, 5, 7 | 351 | about 540 | about 890 |
| Every 4 days | 3 | 273 | about 810 | about 1,080 |

Ordering every 2 days costs the least in total.

**Weak points of the other plans:**
- **Candidates 0 and 2** (every 3 days, 10–20% over forecast for item 1) go over the 228-unit warehouse limit. On the morning of day 10 there would be about 67 units of item 0 plus about 182 of item 1, roughly 249 units, so about 21 units are lost. Their item 1 orders total about 1,078, well above expected demand, which also means extra storage and more overflow.
- **Candidate 7** orders exactly the forecast. Actual demand runs about 4.6% above forecast on average, so it falls short and pays penalties.
- **Candidate 5** has the same 3-day storage cost as the others in that group.
- **Candidates 3 and 7** (and the other 3-day plans): item 0 keeps only 4 days. A 4-day cycle lets none of its safety stock carry over before it expires; a 3-day cycle lets only one day carry over.
- **Candidate 4** orders item 0 every 2 days but item 1 only every 4 days. It pays the same order fees as Candidate 1 but about 350 more in storage for item 1.
- **Candidate 6** saves about 270 in storage but pays about 500 more in order fees than Candidate 1.

**Why Candidate 1 also holds up when demand varies:**
- **Item 1:** it orders 989 units in total against about 939 expected (forecast × 1.046), a small cushion.
- **Item 0:** it orders 541 against about 516 expected.
- Unsold item 0 can still be sold for another 2 days before it expires.
- Total stock stays well under 228, so there is no overflow risk.

I estimate **candidate 1** has the highest expected profit. I worked this out by hand from rough average-value estimates and did not simulate it. Candidate 1's lead over candidate 5 is small, perhaps around 25.

**What all plans share:** the opening stock (27 of product 0 and 58 of product 1) is below the demand for days 0–3. Nothing ordered can arrive before day 3 for product 0 or day 4 for product 1. So every plan loses the same amount at the start.

**How each plan loses money:**
- **Candidate 6** orders every day, 27 times, which costs 39 × 27 ≈ 1053 in order fees. That is about 700 more than a 3-day schedule, and only about 520 of it comes back as lower storage cost. Daily batches also give less protection against bad demand days, so it runs short more often.
- **Candidate 3** orders every 4 days. Product 0 spoils exactly when the next batch arrives, so its leftovers can't roll over. Stock levels and storage costs are high. On day 8 the warehouse holds about 222 of 228 units, so a random high delivery day can overflow. Its product 1 order arriving on day 16 (155) is below the forecast for days 16–19 (170).
- **Candidates 0, 2, 5 and 7** order every 3 days, which costs 351 in order fees. The forecast total demand for product 1 over days 4–29 is 898 units; with the average multiplier of 1.046, expected demand is about 939.
  - Candidate 0 orders 1078 of product 1. That leaves about 140 extra units, or roughly 1250 spent on goods that are never sold, plus storage.
  - Candidate 2 adds a 20% surplus on product 0 as well. On day 10 the warehouse holds about 225 of 228 units, so overflow losses are likely.
  - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast (898), which leaves it about 41 units short of expected demand. Each missed unit costs 7, and random swings make this worse.
  - Candidate 5 (990 of product 1, 543 of product 0) is the best of this group.
- **Candidate 4** orders product 0 every 2 days but product 1 only every 4 days. It pays the same order fees as candidate 1 but keeps more product 1 in stock, costing about 380 more in storage. It also orders less product 1 overall (943).
- **Candidate 1** orders every 2 days. Its totals almost match candidate 5's (989 of product 1, 541 of product 0), and each batch is about 1.1 times the forecast for the 2 days it covers. Five extra orders add about 195 in fees, but average stock drops by about 28 units, saving about 290 in storage. Smaller batches cost about 70 more in product 0 shortages, so the net edge over candidate 5 is about 25. Product 0 leftovers can last into the next cycle because of the 4-day shelf life, and the warehouse never gets close to full.

**Under random demand:** candidate 1 has plenty of room in the warehouse, a steady ~10% surplus, and leftovers that carry into the next cycle. Candidates 0, 2 and 3 can overflow on high delivery days, and candidate 7 has no surplus to absorb high demand.
